parts.context: A lecturer reviews trials of a shorter working week.

transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to examine one of the most discussed ideas in modern working life: the four-day week. It sounds like a luxury, but there is now surprisingly solid evidence about how it works in practice.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: Before I look at the evidence, let me explain why the subject has become so popular. After the pandemic, many employees were reluctant to return to old routines, and employers in some industries found that they had to offer something new to attract and keep good staff.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: The idea of a shorter working week is not new. Back in nineteen twenty-six, the car manufacturer Henry Ford reduced his factory workers' week from six days to five, convinced that rested employees would be more productive.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: In recent years, several large trials have taken place. The biggest, in Britain in twenty twenty-two, involved sixty-one companies and about three thousand employees, who worked four days for the same pay.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: The results were striking. Ninety-two percent of the companies decided to continue the policy, and staff reported less stress and better sleep. Absence due to illness fell by around two thirds.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: These figures come from self-reports as well as company records, and a sceptic might say that people always say they feel better when they are given something for free. That is why researchers also looked at objective measures, such as sick days and staff turnover.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: Revenue stayed broadly stable, which surprised sceptics. One explanation is that employees became more efficient, with shorter meetings and fewer interruptions.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: Some of the companies also reported that recruitment became easier, because the shorter week made their job advertisements more attractive. For small businesses that cannot compete on salary, this can be a real advantage.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: Of course, the four-day week isn't suitable for every sector. Hospitals, for example, need staff around the clock, and some employers worry about customer service in shops and call centres.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: Another concern is that people might simply work longer hours on the four days, which can be tiring. Iceland's experience suggests this can be avoided if the reduction is applied to all the staff and managers plan the workload carefully.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: Sector matters, too. In manufacturing, the pattern of work is often fixed by machines, and in teaching, the timetable is set by the school day. Any change there would have to be designed very differently from a change in an office.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: Critics also argue that the benefits may be temporary, as the excitement of a new arrangement can fade. However, a follow-up study a year later found little change in satisfaction.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: It is also worth noting that most of the trials involved volunteer companies, which were probably more open to change than the average employer. We should therefore be careful about generalising the results to the whole economy.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: So what's my own view? I think the strongest argument is not about productivity at all, but about well-being. If people have more time for family and rest, society benefits in ways that are hard to measure.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ

transcript.text: That's something to keep in mind when you write your essays on this topic. Thank you.
transcript.speaker: PROF DIAZ
